podcast.body: Mozart is used as an example in an analogy to explain the "lack of knowledge" argument against trap music. podcast.title: Performance Analogy by MF Doom
podcast.body: MF Doom used the example of attending "The Marriage of Figaro" without expecting to see Mozart himself to illustrate his philosophy that the art itself, not the physical presence of the artist, is the essence of a performance. "De hecho tu por ejemplo cuando vas a ver las bodas de fígado evidentemente no esperas verte a Mozart y puede ir a disfrutar las bodas de fígado y tampoco es el único que ha ido en este camino."

podcast.title: Scatological Letters and Lyrics
podcast.body: Approximately 12% of Mozart's letters to his friends and associates contained at least one reference to poop. Some of his song lyrics also included scatological content, necessitating changes by other individuals. This aspect of his personality is so notable that it has been speculated to be linked to a case of Tourette's. "Approximately 12% of all Mozart's letters to friends and associates had at least one reference to poop in it."

podcast.title: The Mozart Effect – Enhanced Intellect Theory
podcast.body: The "Mozart effect" is a theory suggesting that exposing fetuses and babies to classical music can enhance a child's intellect in the womb, potentially leading to better math skills, spatial perception, and 8-9 IQ points higher. Studies at various universities appeared to confirm this, leading to the state of Georgia allocating $100,000 annually to provide every newborn with a classical music CD or tape. However, later research, including a 1999 project, questioned the theory, finding that babies received similar benefits from listening to Mozart as from listening to a parent read a Stephen King novel.

xref.title: Classical Piano Training and Influences
xref.body: Trent Reznor received classical music lessons, focusing on "French parlor music" from composers like Mozart, Bach, and Schumann. From this foundation, he later explored Bartok and Debussy, establishing a deep classical background that underpins his later musical endeavors. "Classical music lessons followed with his teacher focusing on what they called French parlor music, which meant Mozart Bach and Schumann. From there, Trent discovered Bartok, Debussy and others."

xref.title: Creative Process Comparison
xref.body: Ash's evolved creative process, characterized by direct "downloads" of musical information, was compared to Mozart's work as described by Salieri in the movie "Amadeus." Salieri noted Mozart's scores had "no eraser marks" or "corrections," suggesting a genius that takes "dictation." "Solary says, when he was looking at Mozart's work, he said, there's no eraser marks. There's no corrections. It's almost like he's taking dictation."

xref.title: Cultural Significance of Scatology
xref.body: Mozart's use of scatological humor in his compositions and letters provides insight into his sense of humor and that of his contemporaries, reinforcing the idea that such humor was more mainstream in 18th-century polite society and contributing to the field of scatter linguistics. "it reinforces the thinking that scatter logical humor was way more mainstream back then, including in polite society than it is today."

xref.title: Lee Mavers' Disappearance and Rumors
xref.body: Following the album's release, Lee Mavers disappeared, leading to various rumors: that he became a painter, went into home decor, became a hopeless heroin addict (though he later recovered), was ceaselessly re-recording old songs, or was living in a monastery where monks praised his musical genius. "And with that, he disappeared. Oh, there were rumors and stories. He'd become a painter, he'd got into home decor, he'd become a hopeless heroin addict. He was re-recording and re-recording songs from that album in a Sisyphean attempt to get them right, that he was living in a monastery, where the resident monks had declared him to be the best thing to happen in music since Mozart."

xref.title: Pain Management Study with Ibuprofen
xref.body: Researchers at the University of Utah conducted a study revealing that listening to Mozart while taking ibuprofen significantly enhances pain relief. While ibuprofen alone reduced inflammation by 70%, the combination with Mozart music further decreased inflammation from 70% to 90%, suggesting a notably greater reduction in pain. Though currently tested on mice, these findings could lead to new human pain management methods if replicated in human trials. "when they gave pain sufferers ibuprofen and had them listen to Mozart at the same time, that inflammation decreased when from 70% to 90%."

xref.title: Sanitized Lyrics Posthumously
xref.body: After Mozart's death, his widow sought to publish his more risqué works like "Lechmik Im Arch," but due to their explicit nature, the lyrics were sanitized for almost 200 years, with the original versions only being widely made public in 1991.
